newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil port workers resume talks with steel firm.
newsitem.headline: Brazil port workers resume talks with steel firm.

text.p: Brazilian port workers were holding fresh talks with steel firm Companhia Siderurgica Paulista (Cosipa) to solve a labor dispute at the company's private terminal at Santos port, officials said.
Negotiations resumed at 1400 local/1700 GMT, the third round of talks since both sides agreed to sit down together to iron out the conflict.
Santos stevedore officials were unavailable to comment on the content of the talks while Cosipa declined to reveal its agenda ahead of the meeting.
But an official at the National Stevedores' Union said Santos union representatives had expressed little hope of resolving the problem ahead of a deadline on April 30.

The stevedores have held two strikes at the port in protest against Cosipa's decision to use its own workers to load and unload vessels at its private terminal. On both occasions, the strike spread to the national level.
"The problem continues to be the same," said Ernani Duarte, secretary general of the national union, explaining that stevedores were refusing to share their work with private workers at the terminal.

Santos Stevedores' Union president Joaquim da Silva said he had little hope of resolving the issue this week, according to Duarte. "He isn't seeing much progress in this direction," Duarte said. Da Silva was unavailable for comment.

The stevedores have proposed a 40 percent cut in their work teams and a reduction in overtime hours for the loading of bulk products. They have also made a separate proposal regarding the loading and unloading of packaged products and containers.
But Cosipa replied that the cost of the stevedores' proposal was still 400 percent higher than that of using its own workers at the terminal.
Although a possibility existed that the port workers would set a new deadline for talks, it was equally probable there would be another port strike, initially at Santos, Duarte said.
"If there is no agreement by April 30...the likelihood is for there to be another strike," he said.
The national union considered that the problem at Santos was not an isolated one and would therefore have to be addressed by the country as a whole, he added.

However, the reading of a bill aiming to reintegrate the terminals of Cosipa and another company, Ultravertil, into Santos port was unlikely to receive a reading soon as Congress was clogged up in slow-moving administrative reforms, he noted.
